nodes.question: What is the mission of the Idaho National Laboratory (INL)?
nodes.answer: The mission of INL is to discover, demonstrate, and secure innovative nuclear energy solutions, other clean energy options, and critical infrastructure.
nodes.paragraph: Idaho National Laboratory (INL), founded in 1949 as heNational Reactor Testing Station, has the mission of discovering, demonstrating, and securing innova- tive nuclear energy solutions, other clean energyoptions, and critical infrastructure. As part of this mission space, post-irradiation examination (PIE) is performed on nuclear fuels and materials to mea-sure their performance and understand the mate-rial behaviors in the extreme temperature and radiation environments of a nuclear reactor. nodes.question: Why is energy access alone not sufficient for choosing clean cooking fuels?
nodes.answer: Energy access alone does not guarantee the availability or affordability of clean cooking fuels, leading to continued use of traditional and polluting sources.

nodes.paragraph: Despite data availability challenges, systematically tracing the inclusivity of COP processes can uncover power dynamics at the highest levels of climate governance. Since its adoption in 1992, the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC) has united the international community to negotiate global climate commitments, particularly at its annual Con - ference of Parties (COP). The UNFCCC process decides by consensus1 to ensure that all signatory countries (Parties) assume common but differentiated responsibilities 2 in climate action, regardless of size or economic capacity3. The UNFCCC secretariat manages accreditation which grants access to official sessions to eligible non-state partici - pants (Observers) from UN agencies, intergovernmental organizations (IGOs) and non-governmental organizations (NGOs). These accredited organizations may freely nominate members for their delegations1, providing restricted access to the negotiation site (blue zone). Those with access can influence broader discourse and negotiations through side events, pavilion events or informal meetings. Non-state actors do not directly participate in decision-making for negotiation texts, but they contribute informally4 by sharing expertise, overseeing the pro - gress of Parties and supporting ambition through a hybrid multilateral governance structure5 7.

nodes.question: How have ECAs contributed to energy systems in recipient countries?
nodes.answer: ECAs have contributed to locking in recipient countries to fossil fuel energy systems, such as coal-fired power stations in Asia and gas infrastructure in Africa.

While capital market actors and multilateral financial institutions have been the subject of significant scholarly attention (Kim and Lee 2021 ; Stoll et al. 2021 ; Ameli et al. 2020 ), public bilateral financial institutions, especially Export Credit Agencies (ECAs), have been largely overlooked (Peterson and Downie 2023 ; Klasen et al. 2022 This is an important oversight given that ECAs are the largest source of bilateral public finance for fossil fuels, which has helped to lock-in recipient countries to fossil fuel energy systems, such as coal fired power stations in Asia and gas infrastructure in Africa (O Manique et al. 2024 ; Chen et al. 2021 ). At the same time, as institutions under the control of national governments, ECAs, unlike private capital or multilateral financial institutions, should be well placed to respond to national climate policy objectives, and use their financial instruments, such as risk insur - ance, to crowd-in private investment for clean energy projects. In this context, it is no surprise that ECAs are facing growing international pressure to align their activities with the goals of the Paris Agreement.

nodes.label: Ethics and regulation
nodes.question: What actions did European ECAs take regarding fossil fuel energy projects in 2022?
nodes.answer: European ECAs committed to ending export credit for fossil fuel energy projects in 2022.
nodes.paragraph: For example, in 2015 OECD countries agreed to restrict export finance for coal-fired power projects (Liao 2021 ). In 2021 European countries launched the Export Finance for Future (E3F) coalition to specifically align export finance with international climate objectives (E3F 2023 ). In the same year, 34 countries signed the Glasgow Statement, which commits signatories to ending public financial support for international fossil fuel projects (DuFour et al. 2022 ). At the national level, many G20 governments have responded by implementing new climate targets. For example, in 2022 European ECAs committed to ending export credit for fossil fuel energy projects (IISD 2022 ), and several other ECAs, including the Export-Import Bank of the US (Exlm) and the UK Export Finance (UKEF) have announced policies to limit public finance for fossil fuels (DuFour et al. 2022 ). While the pressure on ECAs is likely to increase, we do not have a good understanding of the potential for these public bilateral financial institutions to accelerate a clean energy transition.
